plain_english: So let's figure this out. We both agree these things are worth having. But let me explain why I don't count them as truly good things, and how I'd act differently than you if I had them. Put me in charge of a very rich man's house. Surround me with gold and silver dishes used for everyday meals. I won't think I'm a better person because of these things. Even though they're in my house, they're not part of who I am. Now drag me away to the wooden bridge and dump me there with the beggars. I won't look down on myself because I'm sitting with people who hold out their hands for money. What does it matter if you lack a piece of bread when you still have the power to die? So what's my point? I'd rather have the magnificent house than sit on the beggar's bridge. Put me among beautiful furniture and every luxury you can imagine. I won't think I'm any happier just because my cloak is soft or because my guests recline on purple cushions.
original_excerpt: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them. Place me as master in the house of a very rich man: place me where gold and silver plate is used for the commonest purposes; I shall not think more of myself because of things which even though they are in my house are yet no part of me. Take me away to the wooden bridge[5] and put me down there among the beggars: I shall not despise myself because I am sitting among those who hold out their hands for alms: for what can the lack of a piece of bread matter to one who does not lack the power of dying? Well, then? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge. Place me among magnificent furniture and all the appliances of luxury: I shall not think myself any happier because my cloak is soft, because my guests rest upon purple.

plain_english: Let me paint you a different picture: I won't be more miserable if my tired head has to rest on a bundle of hay instead of a soft pillow. I won't suffer more if I have to lie on some torn circus cushion with stuffing poking through the holes. So what's my point? Sure, I'd rather appear in public wearing fine wool and official robes than with bare or half-covered shoulders. I'd like my daily business to go exactly as I want it to. I'd love to have one success follow another. But I won't let myself become proud of this good fortune. Now flip it all around — let losses and grief and all kinds of attacks tear at my spirit. Let every hour bring some new argument or problem. Even surrounded by the worst miseries, I still won't call myself the most wretched person alive. I won't curse any particular day. Why? Because I've made sure I don't have unlucky days.
original_excerpt: Change the scene: I shall be no more miserable if my weary head rests upon a bundle of hay, if I lie upon a cushion from the circus, with all the stuffing on the point of coming out through its patches of threadbare cloth. Well, then? I prefer, as far as my feelings go, to show myself in public dressed in woollen and in robes of office, rather than with naked or half-covered shoulders: I should like every day's business to turn out just as I wish it to do, and new congratulations to be constantly following upon the former ones: yet I will not pride myself upon this: change all this good fortune for its opposite, let my spirit be distracted by losses, grief, various kinds of attacks: let no hour pass without some dispute: I shall not on this account, though beset by the greatest miseries, call myself the most miserable of beings, nor shall I curse any particular day, for I have taken care to have no unlucky days.

plain_english: So what's the point of all this? I'd rather have to control my joys than struggle to overcome my sorrows. The great Socrates would agree with me. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations. Let me ride in Bacchus's golden chariot from sunrise to Thebes. Let Persian kings take laws from me. Even when everyone salutes me as a god, I'll still know I'm just a man. Then connect this peak to a sudden fall into disaster. Put me on a foreign chariot to decorate some cruel conqueror's victory parade. I'll follow behind another's chariot with no more shame than I showed standing in my own. So what then? Despite all this, I'd still rather be the conqueror than the captive. I despise Fortune's entire realm, but if I had to choose, I'd pick the better parts. I'll turn whatever happens to me into something good — but I'd prefer what happens to be comfortable, pleasant, and unlikely to irritate me. Don't think any virtue comes without effort. Some virtues need the spur, others need the reins."
original_excerpt: What, then, is the upshot of all this? it is that I prefer to have to regulate joys than to stifle sorrows. The great Socrates would say the same thing to you. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations: let the voluptuous car of Bacchus bear me in triumph to Thebes from the rising of the sun: let the kings of the Persians receive laws from me: yet I shall feel myself to be a man at the very moment when all around salute me as a God. Straightway connect this lofty height with a headlong fall into misfortune: let me be placed upon a foreign chariot that I may grace the triumph of a proud and savage conqueror: I will follow another's car with no more humility than I showed when I stood in my own. What then? In spite of all this, I had rather be a conqueror than a captive. I despise the whole dominion of Fortune, but still, if I were given my choice, I would choose its better parts. I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb.

plain_english: Think about walking. Sometimes you have to hold yourself back going downhill. Sometimes you have to push yourself hard going uphill. Virtues work the same way. Some virtues are uphill climbs — patience, courage, staying strong when life hits you hard. These virtues have to fight against tough opposition and crush bad luck under their feet. They're climbing, struggling, fighting their way up a steep hill. But other virtues are downhill walks — being generous, moderate, gentle. These flow easily. With the downhill virtues, you have to hold back your spirit so it doesn't run away from you. With the uphill virtues, you have to push and drive yourself forward. So we should use the tough, fighting virtues when we're poor. And we should use the lighter, more careful virtues when we're rich — the ones that move easily and just carry their own weight. Given this difference, I'd rather deal with virtues I can practice in peace than ones I can only test through blood and sweat. "That's why," says the wise man, "I don't say one thing and do another. You just don't understand what I'm saying. You only hear the sound of my words. You don't try to figure out what they actually mean."
original_excerpt: As we have to check our body on a downward path, and to urge it to climb a steep one; so also the path of some virtues leads down hill, that of others uphill. Can we doubt that patience, courage, constancy, and all the other virtues which have to meet strong opposition, and to trample Fortune under their feet, are climbing, struggling, winning their way up a steep ascent? Why! is it not equally evident that generosity, moderation, and gentleness glide easily downhill? With the latter we must hold in our spirit, lest it run away with us: with the former we must urge and spur it on. We ought, therefore, to apply these energetic, combative virtues to poverty, and to riches those other more thrifty ones which trip lightly along, and merely support their own weight. This being the distinction between them, I would rather have to deal with those which I could practise in comparative quiet, than those of which one can only make trial through blood and sweat. "Wherefore," says the sage, "I do not talk one way and live another: but you do not rightly understand what I say: the sound of my words alone reaches your ears, you do not try to find out their meaning."
